Project Proposal

Kaijie Zhang

2026-11-17

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

Vignette 1: Smoking and body mass index (NHANES)

Research question and design

Among US adults, does current smoking, compared with never smoking, lower body mass index (BMI)?

The unit of analysis is the participant, and the population is non-institutionalized US adults aged 20 to 80 (smoking is only recorded from age 20). The exposure is current smoker (1) versus never smoker (0), built from Smoke100 and SmokeNow; former smokers are excluded because quitting can itself change weight. The outcome is BMI (kg/m2), a continuous variable. The confounders, chosen from subject-matter reasoning, are age, sex, race/ethnicity (Race1), education, income-to-poverty ratio (Poverty) and survey cycle. Because age and income may relate to smoking and BMI in non-linear ways, a simple linear adjustment may not be enough.

Data

The data are NHANES 2009-2010 and 2011-2012, collected by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) and distributed in the NHANES R package. I use NHANESraw (20,293 participants) rather than NHANES, because the 10,000-row NHANES table is resampled with replacement and repeats participants (7,235 adult rows but only 4,654 unique IDs), which would distort cross-validation. I will use complete cases and report how many participants are excluded. Descriptive statistics will show the missingness of each variable, BMI by smoking status within age groups, and the confounders by smoking status.

Methods

I will start with the crude difference in mean BMI and a multiple linear regression of BMI on smoking and the confounders. The main estimate comes from the same regression with smooth (spline) terms for age and income.

Machine learning will check whether this adjustment is adequate. Using caret with cross-validation, I will compare how well linear regression, k-nearest neighbors and random forests predict BMI from the confounders. If the flexible models predict clearly better, a linear adjustment is likely not enough. If time permits, I will attempt double machine learning and a causal forest.

Limitations

The data are cross-sectional, so reverse causation is possible, for example weight loss from illness. Smoking is self-reported as yes/no, with no information on how much people smoke, and unmeasured confounders such as diet may remain.

Vignette 2: Permitless carry laws and firearm mortality

Research question and design

Did adopting a permitless carry law change a state’s firearm death rate?

The unit of analysis is the state-year, covering the 50 states and D.C. from 2014 to 2024. The exposure is whether a permitless carry law is in force, starting from its first full calendar year. Twenty-three states adopted such a law between 2016 and 2024; four states that adopted before 2014 are excluded. The outcome is the log age-adjusted firearm death rate, a continuous variable. State and year fixed effects account for stable differences between states and for national trends. The key assumption is parallel trends: without the law, adopting and non-adopting states would have followed similar trends.

Data

gunleg is the RAND Corporation State Firearm Law Database (https://www.rand.org/pubs/tools/TLA243-2-v4.html), with 1,902 records of state firearm laws, their type and effective date. Permitless carry laws are the records with subtype “shall issue (permit not required)”; Texas’s 2021 law is coded “Restrictive” unlike every other state’s, so I define the exposure by subtype. cdcfiremort holds CDC/NCHS age-adjusted firearm death rates per 100,000 by state for 2005 and 2014-2024 (https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/state-stats/deaths/firearms.html). The firearm death rate has no missing values for 2014-2024. Descriptive statistics will show when each state adopted the law and firearm death rates over time for adopting and non-adopting states.

Methods

The main analysis is a regression of the log firearm death rate on a law indicator with state and year fixed effects, with standard errors that allow for correlation within each state. To check the parallel trends assumption, I will add indicators for each year before and after adoption (an event study); the estimates before adoption should be near zero.

Because states adopted in different years, a single regression can be misleading. I will also compare each group of states that adopted in the same year with states that had not yet adopted, and average these comparisons. If time permits, I will try a recently developed difference-in-differences estimator designed for staggered adoption.

Limitations

Adopting states may differ from other states in ways that change over time, which would violate parallel trends. The data are state-level and annual, and the outcome combines firearm suicides and homicides.
